Rules: real_exam/TEACHING_STYLE_GUIDE.md R1-R35 (no 'which way is better' verdict) + NITZAN_RHYTHM_DELIVERY.md P1-P13. Calm preset on the question reading and plain calculations.
slides: Sometimes we can't count everything in one multiplication. Then we split the count into cases, or we subtract.

slides.say: First, something important to know. These questions are rare on the exam, and they are considered hard. Maybe one every few years, and then near the end of the section.

slides: So don't panic. But know the idea, because it also helps a lot in probability, the next topic.

slides.say: Let's start with adding. Now a new example. A lunch is either a sandwich and a drink, or a soup alone.
There are three sandwiches, two drinks and four soups. How many different lunches are possible?

slides: We can't do it in one multiplication, because the two kinds of lunch have different stages. So we split it into two cases.

slides.say: Case one, a sandwich and a drink. Three times two is six lunches.
Case two, a soup alone. That's four lunches.
Every lunch is in one case or the other, never in both. So we add the cases. Six plus four is ten lunches.
Now a new example. A pizza place has four kinds of base and three toppings. A pizza has one base and one topping. But if you take the thin base, the topping must be cheese.
at: A pizza place has four kinds of base

slides: The rule only talks about the thin base. So we split into two cases, the thin base, and any other base.

slides.say: Case one, the thin base. The base has one option, and the topping must be cheese, also one option. One times one is one pizza.
Case two, another base. That's three options. And any topping is allowed, cheese too. Three options. Three times three is nine.
The cases don't overlap, because a base is thin or it isn't. One plus nine is ten pizzas.
Now the other way, subtracting. The same pizzas, but this time we count everything as if there were no rule.
Four bases times three toppings is twelve pizzas.
Which pizzas does the rule forbid? The thin base with the two toppings that aren't cheese. That's two pizzas.
at: The thin base with the two toppings

slides.say: Twelve minus two is ten. The same answer.
So when a rule forbids something, count all of them, and subtract the forbidden ones. All, minus forbidden, leaves what's allowed.
Now a new example. How many two-digit codes can we make from the digits one, two, three and four, if the two digits must be different?
First, all the codes, as if digits could repeat. Four times four is sixteen.
The forbidden codes use the same digit twice. Eleven, twenty-two, thirty-three and forty-four. That's four.
Sixteen minus four is twelve codes.
Let's check it with the pool. The first digit has four options, and then three are left. Four times three is twelve. The same.
And now a type that comes up on the exam. Dan has six shirts, two blue and four white.
He has five pairs of trousers, three blue, one white and one black.
He wears a shirt and trousers that are not the same colour. How many outfits can he wear?
Not the same colour, so let's count all, minus the forbidden. All the outfits are six times five, thirty.
The forbidden ones have the same colour. A blue shirt with blue trousers is two times three, six.
A white shirt with white trousers is four times one, four. No shirt is black, so there's nothing more to forbid.
Six plus four is ten forbidden outfits. Thirty minus ten is twenty.
Let's check it with cases. A blue shirt goes with trousers that aren't blue, two of them. Two times two is four.
A white shirt goes with trousers that aren't white, four of them. Four times four is sixteen. Four plus sixteen is twenty again.
So let's sum it up. If you can't count in one go, split into cases that don't overlap, and add them.
And when you see the words not, different from, or at least one, count all, and subtract the forbidden ones.
at: when you see the words not

slides: Subtracting is worth it when the forbidden group is small and easy to count. Take a moment to memorize this, and I'll see you in the next video.
